$comment: UK SPELLING THROUGHOUT — David's ruling, 2026-08-02. These are British exam papers.
ONE canonical table, like banned-vocabulary.json beside it: read by the shared gates
in content-gates.ts (database sweep + publish doors) and by scripts/scan-vocab.mjs
(the file scan). A second copy would eventually disagree with this one.
SEVERITY IS THE WHOLE DESIGN HERE. An 'error' form does not exist in British English,
so flagging it is safe. A 'warning' form IS a real British word in another sense or
part of speech — 'practice' the noun, 'meter' the gas meter, 'tire' meaning to grow
weary. A scanner cannot tell which sense is meant without parsing the sentence, so it
reports and a person decides. Making those errors would train people to bypass the
gate, which costs more than the misses.
Quoted passage spans and tested tokens are exempt, on the manifesto's ABOUT-language
principle (v1.8): we do not re-spell a quotation, and a spelling item that presents a
US form AS the error to spot is content about the spelling, not a spelling failure.

izeRule.$why: Case-SENSITIVE, and at most one leading capital: `fontSize` and `maxSize` are code identifiers, not American spelling. `Organize` at the start of a sentence still matches.

rules.uk: double the l: travelled, cancelling, jeweller
marvellous · jewellery · skilful · fulfil · fulfilment · enrolment · instalment · counsellor · wilful
grey · plough · mould · smoulder · catalogue · dialogue · aluminium · sulphur · doughnut · pyjamas · aeroplane · cosy · axe · manoeuvre · moustache
noun 'practice', verb 'practise' — check which this is
noun 'licence', verb 'license' — check which this is
the unit is 'metre'; a measuring device is a 'meter'

rules.$why: Only the bare noun is ambiguous. Nobody has ever written 'tyred' or 'tyring', so flagging 'tired' just teaches people to skim the warnings.
rules.uk: the wheel is a 'tyre'; growing weary is 'tire'
the pavement edge is a 'kerb'; restraining is 'curb'
air, beer and animals take 'draught'; a first version is a 'draft'
a floor of a building is a 'storey'
